title: Coq au Vin
subtitle: French chicken braised in red wine with bacon, mushrooms and pearl onions
excerpt: Coq au vin is the great French chicken braise: pieces of chicken browned in bacon fat and then slow-cooked in red wine with mushrooms, pearl onions, and herbs until the wine reduces to a rich, deeply coloured sauce. It is the dish that made French country cooking famous internationally, and it rewards patience -- the longer it cooks, the better it tastes.
sourceNotes: Coq au vin is a classic of French bourgeois cooking, popularised internationally by Julia Child in her 1961 book Mastering the Art of French Cooking. The dish originates in the rural tradition of cooking old roosters (coq) in wine to tenderise the tough meat. Modern versions use chicken thighs or a whole jointed chicken. The recipe here uses the classic Burgundian method.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in the sauce. Reheat gently.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Better the next day. Make up to 2 days ahead.

content.text: Use a whole bottle of red wine. The wine reduces to a concentrated sauce, so start with a full 750 ml. A cheaper red wine that you would drink works well -- something light-to-medium bodied. Do not use a cooking wine. The chicken is best marinated in the wine overnight, though this is optional.

Preheat the oven to 160C. Season {{chicken-thigh}} chicken well with {{salt-table}} salt and {{black-pepper}} pepper. Heat {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil in a large ovenproof pot. Brown the chicken in batches, skin-side down first, until deep golden, about 5 minutes per side. Remove and set aside.

In the same pot, fry {{smoked-bacon}} bacon lardons until crisp, about 4 minutes. Add {{shallots}} shallots and cook for 5 minutes. Add {{garlic}} garlic. Stir in {{plain-flour}} flour and {{tomato-puree}} tomato puree. Cook for 1 minute.

Pour in {{red-wine}} wine and {{chicken-stock}} stock. Add {{thyme-fresh}} thyme and {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves. Return the chicken to the pot, skin-side up. Bring to a simmer. Cover and cook in the oven for 45 minutes.

Saute {{mushrooms-chestnut}} mushrooms in {{unsalted-butter}} butter until golden, about 5 minutes. Add to the pot and continue cooking uncovered for 20 minutes. The sauce should be thick and glossy. Taste for {{salt-table}} salt. Serve with mash or crusty bread.

items.symptom: The sauce is thin and watery
items.cause: The wine needs more time to reduce.
items.fix: Remove the chicken. Boil the sauce hard for 5 to 10 minutes until it thickens and coats the back of a spoon. Return the chicken and serve.

content.text: Coq au vin is a dish of Burgundy and the Lyonnais -- the wine-producing regions of central France. It became known around the world in the second half of the 20th century through the influence of French cooking on restaurant culture. Julia Child's version, published in 1961, was the recipe that brought it into American and British home cooking. It is one of the dishes that defined French cuisine for the international audience.
